RELENTLESS SPIRIT Luis Enrique talks about the improvements both in attack and defence which were key to his Paris Saint-Germain side becoming champions of Europe 15

WI N NING COACH “We have a trait that I think defines us, and that’s that we always keep playing in the same way. Whether we’re winning or losing, the result doesn’t affect us.” With these words, Luis Enrique captures something of the relentless spirit of his Paris Saint-Germain side, a group of players whose unceasing intensity mirrors that of their coach – and which was no better expressed than in May’s Champions League final. On that evening in Munich, Paris achieved the biggest final winning margin in the competition’s history by beating Inter 5-0. However, as Luis Enrique reflects, it was an outcome he could not have dared to dream of back in the winter, when they flirted with early elimination after winning just one – and losing three – of their first five games in the league phase. By the season’s end, though, they had become the first French club to complete a treble of Champions League, Ligue 1 and Coupe de France victories. Here, the 55-year-old reflects on the thrilling run that took them from that tentative start to their triumphant finish, sealing a maiden Champions League title for his club and a second for himself as a coach, ten years after his first conquest of Europe with Barcelona. If we look back to your team’s position after Matchday 5, could you have imagined that you would win the Champions League and make history by winning it so decisively? It would be very difficult go that far because, normally, elite football is played based on the current mood, and the time you’re talking about was a very precarious one when the objective was to advance to the next round – to advance as one of the top 24, not to win the Champions League. ROA D T O M U NICH The 2024/25 UEFA Champions League commenced with the competition’s inaugural league phase, which ran between 17 September and 29 January. This was a departure from the long-established group-stage concept first introduced in 1991/92 and it meant that, rather than a cluster of four-team groups, there was instead a single 36-team league in which each side played eight matches – four home and four away. Overall, 144 games were played and 16 national associations were represented though, amid the novelties, a familiar face finished top in the form of a Liverpool side victorious in their first seven matches. Another change was the play-off round that followed in the new year, prior to the round of 16, and with more games there was no shortage of talking points for UEFA’s Technical Observer Group – as reflected in the following section-by-section analysis of this season’s competition. ROUND OF 16 REAL MADRID v ATLÉTICO DE MADRID The pursuit of control was a prominent theme in the meeting of Madrid’s big two Eduardo Camavinga tackles Ángel Correa MANAGING THE GAME Control was the word on the lips of both Carlo Ancelotti and Diego Simeone over the course of a tightly contested UEFA Champions League round of 16 encounter between Real Madrid and Atlético de Madrid. Both coaches used it after a first leg of few chances had finished 2-1 to Los Blancos, largely thanks to the individual quality of the goalscorers. And for UEFA’s Technical Observer Group, the way in which the two men ‘managed’ that opening game held particular intrigue – starting with Madrid’s approach in possession. SCULPTING SKILLS Our technical team presents four drills to help coaches prepare their teams for the evolving demands of the game Insights gathered during the UEFA Champions League have been translated into practical guidance for elite youth development. By analysing performance data and emerging trends from senior club matches, our experts have identified key themes to shape targeted training sessions. The four exercises outlined here are designed to reflect these current developments, helping players stay equipped for the game’s modern challenges. 111

CREATING OVERLOADS SESSION ORGANISATION COACHING POINTS • 20 players + 2 goalkeepers • Find free man using mobility and third-man moves • Yellow team always start with the ball from goal kick • Unbalance the opponent changing sides and making opposite moves (support and deep) • First zone 9 + GK vs 7, take advantage of numerical superiority to find a way to connect to final third. • Change rhythm when they find the opportunity and gain Two pocket players can come down the advantage on the field • In the red zone blue team can defend with • Correctly occupy the box and areas around 4 Defenders + 1 Midfielder + Goalkeeper • Blues to score in opposite goal after regaining possession 113

C OACH ING D R ILLS PRESSING TO FORCE OUTSIDE SESSION ORGANISATION COACHING POINTS • 10 players + 2 goalkeepers • Close the middle and direct press from inside to outside • Playing dimensions 36m x 42m; Goals in middle 2m wide / 3m distance; Repetitions 3 x 4 minutes • Aggressive press: maximum intensity in run-ups • Blue starts from Goalkeeper; Goals count on big goal and • Close spaces at the back, create equality / superiority passing goals (1 point each) • Fight duels with the aim of winning the ball • Yellow presses and aims to recover the ball as high as possible and score in big goal within 7 seconds • Variation: build-up team can only use Goalkeeper once; Ball can no longer be played behind the red zone; only waist-high passes allowed; goals scored in big goals count double 114 2 0 24/ 25 U EFA C H A M P I O N S L EAGUE TEC HN IC A L REPORT

With the game locked at 0-0 and Barcelona increasingly building attacking momentum, Arsenal coach Renée Slegers made a decisive double change that would shift the rhythm of the game and give the north London side their first European trophy in 18 years. With 67 minutes played, Slegers withdrew forwards Frida Maanum and Chloe Kelly, introducing Blackstenius and Mead from the bench. The changes triggered a small tactical adjustment that would prove crucial in deciding who would lift the trophy in Lisbon. As part of the reshuffle, Arsenal centre-forward Alessia Russo, who had worked tirelessly at the top of the pitch, dropped into the deeper position previously occupied by Maanum. With Russo now looking to connect the game from a more withdrawn position, Blackstenius was free to work up against Barcelona’s back line. “When Stina came into the game, she stretched the game a lot more,” explained Gemma Grainger, UEFA Technical Observer. “It meant Barcelona’s defenders had to be aware of this threat in behind the back line and moved their positioning a little bit deeper. She stretched the game. “Her ability to threaten behind Barcelona continued to impact the game,” added Grainger. “It helped Arsenal move up the pitch and gain territory in the opposition’s half. Arsenal were able to win possession higher up the pitch and started to win free-kicks in Barcelona’s half. text: WI N NING COACH Looking back on the season, what were some of the games that jumped out at you as the biggest challenges? Different games have different challenges, and I think what’s been so good about this team is that we’ve wanted to overcome those challenges. There are a couple of key moments. Of course, the Bayern München game at home, because I think that’s when we started to show how we wanted to try and get wins over the line. [Regarding] Lyon, I think we spoke about not knowing how we’re going to do against these teams. But what the players also said after the first 30 minutes in the home game against them helped us understand that we can compete with these teams. We can do it. And I think the learning for the future would be to do it from minute one, because we know we can believe in ourselves. And I think the speed of the progress we’ve made, then being able to apply that in the away leg with a lot of pressure on us and winning 4-1 [says a lot]. Holders Barcelona were joined in the group stage by fellow former champions Arsenal, Lyon and Wolfsburg while Galatasaray and Hammarby made their competition debuts. Celtic, Manchester City, Twente and Vålerenga appeared in the group stage for the first time. T H EO RY I N TO P RACT I C E SUPPORTING THE COACHES The UEFA Coaching Convention sets minimum standards for national associations and offers them guidance, information and support The UEFA Coaching Convention provides a benchmark Lazio players during for the education of coaches within Europe, helping to a training session raise the quality of coaching across the continent and facilitating the free movement of qualified professionals around UEFA’s member associations. The value of Article 8 of the convention is worth highlighting as it promotes reality-based learning – a key tool for coaches today. Informal learning UEFA supports informal learning – learning that is incidental or self-directed and not led by another person. Examples include everyday experiences, observing or talking to other coaches and self-study. The more insights coaches gain, the better they can discover what works for them in practice. Understanding how to apply knowledge in coaching is a key part of development. Reality-based learning Reality-based learning is beneficial because by ensuring the learning environment is realistic, coaches can prepare themselves and their players for the real-life situations they may face. As UEFA technical instructor Phil Church said: “If you don’t do reality-based Imanol Alguacil training, you won’t create problem-solving players.” By and David Hubert replicating matchday situations, coaches offer players chat before their sides face off the chance to develop the tools required to make quick and effective decisions in a safe environment. 92 2024/ 25 U EFA EU ROPA LEAGU E TECHNICAL REPORT

Structured practice provides more control to create the pictures they want to see but should not restrict decision-making. Opposition analysis can offer insight, but coaches must adapt to challenges on matchday. This may involve tactical changes or substitutions. In the UEFA Conference League final, Chelsea coach Enzo Maresca introduced Jadon Sancho, a winger who dribbles and drives forward. As Church said: “He makes the defence drop, which is a different tactical problem.” Coaches should create environments where players identify problems and find solutions. Kris Van Der Haegen, coach education director at the Belgian FA, said: “You need to give them the space to try out what they have. If they recognise the structure of the opposition and they know their role, they can express themselves in a creative way.” Unstructured moments such as transition are harder to prepare for. The value of Article 8 of the convention is worth highlighting as it promotes reality-based learning – a key tool for coaches today. Informal learning UEFA supports informal learning – learning that is incidental or self-directed and not led by another person. Examples include everyday experiences, observing or talking to other coaches and self-study. The more insights coaches gain, the better they can discover what works for them in practice. Understanding how to apply knowledge in coaching is a key part of development. Reality-based learning Reality-based learning is beneficial because by ensuring the learning environment is realistic, coaches can prepare themselves and their players for the real-life situations they may face. Opposition analysis can offer insight, but coaches must adapt to challenges on matchday. This may involve tactical changes or substitutions. TECHNICAL ANALYSIS FITNESS The UEFA Fitness Group put the teams’ physical data under the microscope, with high-intensity output up significantly and some marked variations according to position and tactics Towards the end of her press conference after England’s final victory, Sarina Wiegman began a reflection that went beyond England’s Michelle her own team’s exploits to touch on broader tournament Agyemang on the run trends. And it was telling that she soon landed on the physical aspect of the matches in Switzerland, declaring: “The intensity of the games went through the roof.” That assertion from the winning coach of the last three Women’s EUROs aligned with the view of the UEFA Technical Observer Group, with Anna Signeul highlighting this aspect when she said: “I’ve been immensely impressed by the intensity of the games and the fitness level of the players. In the three years since the previous EURO, the fitness level has increased very much.” Intensity is the apposite word. The average total distance covered per player at this tournament was actually lower than in 2022 yet high-intensity output increased. By way of example, the average distance covered by wingers when running at high speed in Switzerland was 799m per game, compared to 588m in 2022. In other words, wingers sprinted 200m more per game on average than they had done at the previous Women’s EURO. Another example comes from the players in the midfield pivot/No6 position whose average distance covered increased by 1.3km per game to 10.8km – the highest output of any position. COACHING DRILLS BUILDING FROM THE BACK Session organisation Coaching points • 20 players + 2 goalkeepers • Attract the pressure and then find free player to connect over the first lines of press • Orange team always start with the ball from goal kick • Third-man combination: support vs deep moves • Yellow team to advance the ball and attack with numerical advantage (5 vs 4 + Goalkeeper) • Create advantages that can be used to play forward • Purple team to regain the ball and counter towards the • Create overloads from behind: be proactive opposite goal • Play under pressure • Vertical moves after winning the advantage 88 UEFA WOMEN’S EURO 2025 | T E C H N I C A L R E P O R T

THIRD-PLAYER COMBINATIONS Session organisation Coaching points • 19 players total: 9 attackers + GK (Orange), 7 defenders + GK (Purple) • Third-player combinations: Emphasise using central and 1 neutral player (always supports team in possession) players (Zone B) as links to break lines and commit opponents • Set up a pitch divided into three vertical zones (A–B–C) • Attract and release: Use Zone B intentionally to • The Orange team (9 players) always start in possession draw defenders out of position before switching or advancing • Neutral player supports the team in possession and can move freely across zones • Neutral player’s role: Provide support between lines to maintain circulation and enable combination play • Rules for Orange (in possession): • Defensive transition: Encourage quick reactions on - If the ball travels from Zone A to Zone B, the players in Zone B must loss of possession — nearest player applies pressure, return the ball to Zone A (to attract pressure) others cover and delay - If the ball goes directly from Zone A to Zone C, players in Zone C must combine with a third-player action via Zone B before freely attacking - Once a third-player combination is achieved through Zone B, Zone B players can join the attack into Zone C • Rules for Purple (out of possession): - Defenders can move freely across all zones - Upon regaining possession, their objective is to counterattack and score as quickly as possible 89

COACHING DRILLS WIDE PLAY AND OVERLOAD Session organisation Coaching points • 10 + 6 + 1 Goalkeeper • Side pocket players must run in behind full-back • Orange team always start with the ball • Choice for wide players is to play the ball for the deep run or play the ball backwards to the edge player • Must switch the play from one side to the other before attacking – they can switch multiple times if needed • If the player tracks the run of the player in behind and the cross is blocked – option to play back to edge player to cross from half- • Purples start on edge of box and can defend “live” space outside the box • Oranges have to score from a cutback or ball played back to half- • Details on crossing to beat first defender space outside the box + cross • Timing of runs from opposite side in between gaps • Second balls: rest defence to maintain the attack 90 UEFA WOMEN’S EURO 2025 | T E C H N I C A L R E P O R T

DEFENSIVE COMPACTNESS Session organisation Coaching points • 19 players + 1 goalkeeper • Pressing triggers within the block: when and where to press, forcing backwards • Orange team build from the back and aim to progress through the pitch • Defending concepts: body position, orientation, aggressiveness, distances • Orange team score by finishing in the big goal • Lines coordination: press, cover and balance, closing • Purple team defend in mid-block central lanes • When Purple team regain the ball, they can score • Offensive transition: speed and quality of execution in either of the three mini goals 91
